title: Inside Georgia's Push to Rebuild Trust in Elections
summary:
In a small warehouse in Paulding County, Georgia, about an hour west of Atlanta, workers are unpacking voting machines and running tests for logic and accuracy. The checks are part of a statewide routine as Georgia prepares for midterm elections next month, designed to make sure every vote is counted correctly.

At the county election headquarters, equipment is organized and sent out to polling places. The ballot scanners, made by Dominion Voting Systems, are each secured and locked in six different places to prevent tampering. Lacy Dunn, the assistant elections director in Paulding County, says workers test every race, every candidate, every piece of equipment, and every ballot.

Overseeing the work statewide is Brad Raffensperger, Georgia's Republican secretary of state for the past eight years. He says his team stays in daily contact with all 159 counties, focusing on training, oversight, and steady communication.

Georgia has been at the center of a national debate about elections ever since President Donald Trump made false claims about the state's role in the 2020 election. Raffensperger became widely known for refusing to help Trump overturn the 2020 result in Georgia. In January of this year, FBI agents searched the Fulton County election headquarters and seized hundreds of boxes of 2020 election material. Almost nine months later, the FBI has yet to bring charges.

The debate has left some voters unsure. One voter said they believe there may have been a problem in 2020, while another said they feel optimistic that their vote will be counted this time. Now, in the last election he will oversee, Raffensperger is pushing back on efforts by the Trump administration to take more control over elections. Georgia, like 30 other states, refused to turn over sensitive voter information to the Department of Justice.
why_it_matters: People need to believe their votes are counted correctly for election results to be accepted and for voters to keep taking part.

background_read: Elections are how voters choose the people who will hold public office.
Voting machines and ballot scanners record and count the votes that people cast.
Before voting begins, election workers test the equipment to check that every race, candidate, and ballot is handled correctly.
When voters trust that votes are counted correctly, they are more likely to trust the result of an election.

KEY EVENT: Statewide checks of voting equipment, run from county headquarters and overseen by the secretary of state.

├─ WHAT: Unpacking voting machines, running logic and accuracy tests, and locking ballot scanners in six places.
└─ WHERE: A warehouse and the election headquarters in Paulding County, Georgia, with work across all 159 counties.
